resources.string: How muscle satellite cells renew and repair
A simplified view of satellite cells in adult skeletal muscle. Sizes, shapes and timing are schematic. Renewal and fusion are possible outcomes, not a fixed pair of fates for every division.
A resting cell beneath the basal lamina

A resting satellite cell sits between the basal lamina, a thin outer layer, and the sarcolemma, the muscle fiber’s own cell membrane. The satellite cell has a nucleus of its own and is separate from the fiber.
When nearby muscle needs repair, signals from the surrounding tissue can activate satellite cells. An activated cell leaves its resting state and can begin dividing.
The activated satellite cell divides into two daughter cells, each with its own nucleus. Further divisions can produce more descendants. The muscle fiber itself is not dividing.
Some descendants settle back beneath the basal lamina as resting satellite cells. This self-renewal keeps a reserve for future repair. Other descendants develop into muscle-forming cells.
A descendant joins the muscle fiber
A muscle-forming descendant can fuse with an existing fiber. Their membranes join and the descendant’s nucleus becomes one of the fiber’s many nuclei. The resting satellite cell remains separate.
